Modern monetary policy rests on a puzzle that earlier generations of economists, accustomed to thinking of policy as a sequence of sensible decisions, largely overlooked. In 1977 Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott showed that a policy which is optimal when it is announced may cease to be optimal when the time comes to carry it out. Suppose a government announces that it will keep inflation low. Wage-setters, believing the announcement, negotiate modest pay rises. Once those wages are fixed, however, the government faces a temptation: a burst of unexpected inflation would reduce real wages, stimulate hiring and lower unemployment, at least for a while. Since workers can foresee this temptation, they do not believe the original announcement, and they bargain for higher wages in anticipation. The outcome is the worst of both worlds: inflation is higher than anyone wished, and unemployment is no lower than it would have been had the government simply kept its word. The problem is called time inconsistency, and its lesson is uncomfortable: a government’s discretion can be a liability precisely because it is a freedom that others know it possesses. The structure is that of Odysseus and the sirens: the sailor who knows he will be tempted does best to have himself bound to the mast beforehand.

The remedy suggested by the theory is to tie the government’s hands. One way is to adopt a fixed rule, but rules are brittle, since no rule can anticipate every shock. A more flexible alternative, proposed by Kenneth Rogoff in 1985, is to delegate monetary policy to an independent central banker who is known to dislike inflation more than society as a whole does. Such an appointee will resist the temptation to inflate, workers will anticipate this, and the inflationary bias disappears, at the cost of somewhat less stabilisation when shocks strike. The delegation logic carries its own risk: an appointee too averse to inflation may impose needless unemployment, so that the ideal delegate is conservative rather than fanatical. Over the following decades, a wave of legislative reforms granted operational independence to central banks in dozens of countries, often paired with explicit inflation targets. Cross-country comparisons from the 1970s and 1980s seemed to vindicate the strategy: among advanced economies, those with more independent central banks recorded lower average inflation without suffering slower growth.

The evidence, however, is more delicate than the enthusiasm it inspired. A correlation between independence and low inflation does not establish that independence produced low inflation. The most independent central bank of the period, the German Bundesbank, operated in a society scarred by the hyperinflation of the 1920s, in which public aversion to inflation was intense and would have constrained any government, whatever the formal statutes said. Independence, on this reading, is not a cause but a symptom: countries that dislike inflation both create independent central banks and elect governments that refrain from meddling with them. Reverse causation is also possible, since governments may grant independence after inflation has already been subdued, as a way of locking in gains rather than achieving them. A further complication is that in many developing economies formal independence on paper has borne little relation to practice; where governors are dismissed at will, statutory independence is decorative, and the measured correlation weakens accordingly.

The global financial crisis of 2008 and its aftermath raised a different difficulty. To prevent collapse, and later to stimulate recovery once interest rates approached zero, central banks bought vast quantities of government bonds and other assets. These purchases blurred the boundary between monetary and fiscal policy, and their effects were unmistakably distributional: they raised the prices of financial assets, benefiting those who owned them, and lowered the returns on savings. The case for independence had always rested on the claim that monetary policy is a technical task, best insulated from political time horizons. But an institution whose decisions redistribute wealth is exercising political judgement, and the more its mandate expands to cover financial stability, employment or even climate risk, the harder it becomes to explain why its choices should be shielded from the democratic scrutiny applied to other public bodies. Nor is the concern merely theoretical: legislatures in several countries have begun to question central-bank balance sheets and to propose changes to mandates, precisely because tools once deemed technical now carry visible winners and losers.

The surge in inflation that followed the pandemic tested the doctrine from the opposite direction. Central banks were criticised for describing the early price rises as transitory and for acting late. Yet longer-term inflation expectations, as measured in bond markets and surveys, remained largely anchored even as actual inflation rose sharply, and this was widely credited to the credibility built over preceding decades. The interpretation is contestable. It may be that anchoring reflected credibility earned; it may equally be that the shocks were understood to be temporary, or that expectations are slow to adjust for reasons unrelated to any institution’s reputation. Credibility has an awkward property: it is a stock that is invisible in calm conditions and can be inferred only from how expectations behave when a central bank is tempted, or even forced, to deviate from its stated path. Because such episodes are rare and each has its own confounding circumstances, no single one can settle whether the asset is real.

What emerges is a tension that no institutional design fully dissolves. Credibility argues for commitment: the more predictably a central bank behaves, the more its promises can be believed. Flexibility argues for discretion: a bank that cannot look through a temporary supply shock will inflict needless unemployment in the name of consistency. The practical resolution, sometimes called constrained discretion, is to commit firmly to an objective while retaining freedom over the means and, within limits, the speed of return to target. The arrangement works only so long as the public trusts the bank to use its flexibility for the reasons it states. A central bank that draws too often on that trust to excuse deviations will find the reserve exhausted precisely when it is most needed, and because the reserve cannot be seen, the depletion will be noticed only after it is complete.
questions.question: In the time-inconsistency model described in the passage, a government’s announcement of a low-inflation target fails to secure low inflation because:
options: A) governments cannot in practice influence inflation at all, so any announced target is a promise beyond their power to keep or to honour
B) wage-setters distrust the statistical agencies that measure inflation, and therefore bargain for higher pay whatever target has been announced by ministers
C) wage-setters foresee that the government will gain from surprise inflation once wages are fixed, so they discount the announcement
D) unemployment always falls when inflation rises, so governments invariably prefer higher inflation to the low inflation they announce in advance to voters
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 1: once wages are fixed, unexpected inflation lowers real wages and unemployment, so the government is tempted; workers anticipate the temptation and do not believe the announcement. The other options add claims (no control over inflation, distrust of agencies, 'always' and 'invariably') that the model does not make.

questions.question: According to the passage, delegating policy to a central banker who is more averse to inflation than society is improves outcomes chiefly because:
options: A) his known preferences make it credible that he will resist surprise inflation, so expectations and wage demands stay low
B) he has superior technical knowledge of the economy, which lets him forecast shocks more accurately than any elected government could manage
C) he is barred from responding to shocks at all, which removes the stabilisation cost that discretion would otherwise impose on society at large
D) he is appointed for a fixed term, which guarantees that inflation will never rise above the announced target during any period

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the inference that central-bank independence causes lower inflation?
options: A) Countries with independent central banks in the 1970s and 1980s also tended to have larger public sectors than countries without them.
B) Independent central banks in advanced economies sometimes raised interest rates when unemployment was high, at a cost to output in those years.
C) Cross-country data on inflation are available for more advanced economies than for developing economies with weaker institutions in that period.
D) Most countries granted independence to their central banks only after inflation had already been brought down by other means.
questions.explanation: Explanation: This is reverse causation: if low inflation preceded independence, independence cannot be what produced it (paragraph 3 raises exactly this possibility). The other options concern side facts that do not touch the causal claim.

questions.question: The argument of the fourth paragraph implies that the case for central-bank independence:
options: A) collapses because unconventional asset purchases proved to be ineffective at preventing financial collapse or at supporting later recovery
B) weakens as central-bank decisions come to carry distributional consequences resembling those of political choices
C) was never based on technical grounds, but only on a desire to protect financial institutions from public accountability and scrutiny
D) is strengthened whenever a central bank takes on additional mandates, since more complex tasks require greater insulation from politicians
questions.explanation: Explanation: The case for independence rested on monetary policy being a technical task; once decisions redistribute wealth, they are political judgements and the insulation is harder to defend. The passage does not say the purchases were ineffective, and it says the opposite of the last option.

questions.question: The author describes credibility as “invisible in calm conditions” in order to suggest that:
options: A) credibility is a fiction created by central bankers to justify their independence, since it cannot be observed under any conditions at all
B) anchored expectations after the pandemic prove that credibility was genuine and that earlier criticism of central banks was unjustified
C) its existence can be inferred only from how expectations behave when a central bank is tempted or forced to deviate from its path

For much of the twentieth century, ecologists debated what limits the abundance of animals in nature. The orthodox answer looked from the bottom up: plants capture the sun’s energy, herbivores are limited by the supply of plants, and predators are limited by the supply of herbivores. In 1960, three American ecologists, Nelson Hairston, Frederick Smith and Lawrence Slobodkin, proposed a provocative inversion. The world is green, they argued, because herbivores are usually held in check by predators, and are therefore seldom numerous enough to strip the vegetation on which they feed. Control, on this account, runs from the top down. The idea was soon given experimental support by Robert Paine, who removed the starfish Pisaster from stretches of rocky Pacific shoreline and watched mussels, released from predation, crowd out other species until diversity collapsed. Paine coined the term keystone species to describe a predator whose influence far exceeds its abundance, and later gave the general phenomenon its name: the trophic cascade.

The most celebrated modern illustration is the return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996, after roughly seventy years of absence. In the popular version of the story, which has been told in documentaries and viral videos, the wolves reduced the numbers of elk and, just as importantly, frightened them away from vulnerable riverbanks. Willows and aspens, freed from browsing, recovered; beavers, which depend on willows, returned; streams narrowed and stabilised; songbirds and fish flourished. The wolf became an emblem of ecological restoration, and its lesson was taken up by the rewilding movement, which argues that restoring lost predators and other keystone species can repair ecosystems more cheaply and durably than continuous human management. It is an appealing argument, in part because it promises that nature, once given the chance, will do most of the work.

Yet field ecologists have grown uneasy about how much of this narrative the evidence can bear. Elk numbers in the park had begun to decline before the wolves arrived, owing in part to changes in hunting policy outside the park boundaries, and continued to fall as bears, cougars and human hunters took their share; the contribution of wolves to the decline is therefore difficult to isolate. The recovery of willows has been uneven, strong in some drainages and negligible in others, and appears to depend on local hydrology, snow depth and browsing history as much as on the presence of predators. The “landscape of fear”, in which elk avoid dangerous places rather than dying in large numbers, is plausible in principle, but studies of whether elk actually changed their behaviour have produced conflicting results. And the claim that wolves altered the physical course of rivers rests on still thinner evidence. The story’s persuasive power, critics say, has outrun its data.

A deeper problem is methodological. Paine’s starfish were removed from some plots and left in others, so that the difference between them could be attributed to the manipulation. Yellowstone offers no such comparison. There is no matched park without wolves, and the before-and-after contrast is confounded by every other change that happened over the same decades, including climate, hunting rules and the recovery of other predators. Moreover, what counts as a “natural” baseline is itself uncertain: ecologists working after a century of human disturbance may be describing recovery towards a state that never existed in the form imagined. Ecologists distinguish sharply between experiments, in which the investigator controls the cause, and natural histories, in which the investigator infers a cause from a sequence of events; the latter can be illuminating without being decisive. That a story is coherent is not evidence that it is true, and coherence is the very quality that makes stories memorable.

Nothing here shows that trophic cascades are illusory. Where food webs are simple and species interactions strong, as in some lakes and kelp forests, the evidence is compelling: when sea otters disappeared from stretches of the Pacific coast, urchins multiplied and devoured the kelp that sheltered fish. In systems with many species, omnivores and alternative feeding routes, however, effects tend to be diffused, so that removing one predator changes less than the tidy model predicts. The lesson may be less that predators do not matter than that their importance depends on the structure of the web in which they sit.

European rewilding projects illustrate the same difficulty on a smaller scale. Beavers reintroduced to parts of Britain have been credited with slowing floodwaters and creating wetlands, and there are measurements supporting these claims at particular sites; yet the same animals have flooded farmland and felled valued trees elsewhere. Such divergent outcomes are not evidence of failure so much as reminders that ecological effects are contingent on landscape, land use and the presence of other species. Defenders of rewilding accordingly emphasise adaptive management, in which interventions are treated as experiments with monitoring and the possibility of revision, an approach that concedes exactly the humility that the most enthusiastic popular accounts lack.

The stakes extend beyond ecology. Reintroductions impose costs on people who live alongside the animals, such as ranchers who lose livestock, while the benefits, whether biodiversity, tourism or ecological services, are diffuse and often accrue to distant beneficiaries. When the ecological case is presented as certain, the resulting policy commits local communities to bearing costs on the strength of a story that may be partly wrong; when it is presented honestly as probable and context-dependent, it invites a harder but healthier conversation about compensation, monitoring and the willingness to reverse course. The temptation in conservation, as in other fields with public appeal, is to tell the simple story because it wins support. The risk is that support won by a simple story is fragile, and may collapse when the complications become known.

A state cannot govern what it cannot see. To tax property, it needs to know who owns what; to conscript soldiers, it needs to know who lives where and how old they are; to deliver schooling or vaccination, it needs a census. The political scientist James C. Scott, in Seeing Like a State, argued that modern states have therefore been engaged for centuries in a project of legibility: the simplification of a messy, local social reality into standardised categories that can be read from the centre. Permanent surnames, cadastral maps, uniform weights and measures, and standardised languages of administration are all, in this sense, technologies of legibility. Turkey’s Surname Law of 1934, which required citizens to adopt fixed family names, made individuals easier to trace as well as more modern in self-presentation. Before such simplification, local arrangements such as customary land tenure, shifting patterns of grazing and cultivation, and unwritten rules of access to the commons were often opaque to outsiders, yet functional to those who lived within them. What made them functional was precisely what made them unreadable: they were adapted to particular soils, particular seasons and particular relationships that no standard form could capture.

Scott’s parable of the scientific forest illustrates the hazards. In late eighteenth-century Prussia and Saxony, foresters trained to see woodland as a source of timber revenue reorganised natural forests into even-aged plantations of a single species, planted in straight rows to make counting and harvesting easy. The immediate results were impressive, with high yields of uniform timber. Scott, drawing on forestry historians, argues that the costs emerged only later: the simplified stands, stripped of the tangle of undergrowth, fungi, insects and dead wood that had sustained the soil, proved vulnerable to disease and to declining fertility in successive rotations. The forest had been made legible at the price of the very complexity that had kept it productive. The deeper lesson, in Scott’s view, is that the map gradually replaces the territory: what the administrator can measure comes to define what is valued, and what cannot be measured is treated as waste.

Twentieth-century urban planning offered a grander version of the same error. Le Corbusier’s vision of the modern city, with its towers, functional zoning and broad highways, was designed to be grasped at a glance from above, and Brasília, built from nothing in the 1950s, is its most complete realisation. Against this, Jane Jacobs argued in The Death and Life of Great American Cities that the vitality of a neighbourhood arises from things the planner’s plan cannot see: short blocks, buildings of different ages, mixed uses, and the ceaseless small transactions of people on pavements. What the planner perceived as disorder was, for Jacobs, an order too intricate to survey. Scott borrowed from the Greek a word for such practical knowledge, metis, the craft skill that comes from experience and cannot be reduced to rules, and he argued that high-handed planning repeatedly destroyed the stock of metis on which ordinary life depended.

It would be wrong, however, to read Scott as an enemy of legibility as such, and he does not present himself as one. The modern welfare state is unimaginable without it. A person who is not recorded, who lacks a birth certificate, an address or an identity document, cannot readily claim a pension, enrol a child in school, or receive relief after a flood. For such people illegibility is not freedom but exclusion, and it is the poor who suffer most from it. The paradox is that the same standardisation that lets a state serve its citizens also lets it control them; there is no register that can be used for benefit but not for surveillance, no census that can identify the needy without also identifying the taxable. The question is therefore never whether to record, but on what terms.

What distinguishes the catastrophes in Scott’s examples, such as Soviet collectivisation and compulsory village settlement in Tanzania, is not legibility alone but a conjunction of four ingredients. The first is the administrative ordering of nature and society. The second is a “high-modernist” ideology, a supreme confidence in scientific and technical progress. The third is an authoritarian state willing and able to impose its plans by coercion. The fourth is a prostrate civil society, unable to resist. It follows that the third and fourth conditions carry much of the explanatory weight: where citizens can protest, courts can intervene and local knowledge can be voiced, the same tools of legibility may be far less dangerous. That implication is often lost by those who cite Scott against any form of public planning.

Critics have pressed a different objection: that Scott romanticises local knowledge. Customary arrangements were sometimes hierarchical and oppressive, and the legibility that flattened them could liberate individuals from them. Registration of births and marriages, individual land titles and standard courts of law have in various places extended rights to women, low-caste cultivators and minorities whom local elites had kept invisible. To defend the local against the central is thus not necessarily to defend the vulnerable. There is a further irony: Scott’s own analysis depends on official records, the very archives of legibility, and on the accounts of foresters and planners who left detailed written descriptions of their projects, whereas the practices they displaced are known mainly through the eyes of outsiders. The critic of the map relies on maps. The better question, on this view, is not whether a society should be legible but to whom, for what purpose, and with what accountability. A map is neither friendly nor hostile; what matters is who holds it, who was consulted in drawing it, and whether those who appear on it can contest what it says.

The paradox is that the same standardisation that lets a state serve its citizens also lets it control them; there is no register that can be used for benefit but not for surveillance, no census that can identify the needy without also identifying the taxable. The question is therefore never whether to record, but on what terms.

What distinguishes the catastrophes in Scott’s examples, such as Soviet collectivisation and compulsory village settlement in Tanzania, is not legibility alone but a conjunction of four ingredients. The first is the administrative ordering of nature and society. The second is a “high-modernist” ideology, a supreme confidence in scientific and technical progress. The third is an authoritarian state willing and able to impose its plans by coercion. The fourth is a prostrate civil society, unable to resist. It follows that the third and fourth conditions carry much of the explanatory weight: where citizens can protest, courts can intervene and local knowledge can be voiced, the same tools of legibility may be far less dangerous. That implication is often lost by those who cite Scott against any form of public planning.

Critics have pressed a different objection: that Scott romanticises local knowledge. Customary arrangements were sometimes hierarchical and oppressive, and the legibility that flattened them could liberate individuals from them. Registration of births and marriages, individual land titles and standard courts of law have in various places extended rights to women, low-caste cultivators and minorities whom local elites had kept invisible. To defend the local against the central is thus not necessarily to defend the vulnerable. There is a further irony: Scott’s own analysis depends on official records, the very archives of legibility, and on the accounts of foresters and planners who left detailed written descriptions of their projects, whereas the practices they displaced are known mainly through the eyes of outsiders. The critic of the map relies on maps. The better question, on this view, is not whether a society should be legible but to whom, for what purpose, and with what accountability. A map is neither friendly nor hostile; what matters is who holds it, who was consulted in drawing it, and whether those who appear on it can contest what it says.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most support the criticism that Scott romanticises local knowledge?
options: A) Land-registration reforms in several regions gave women enforceable property rights that customary tenure had denied them.
B) Planned cities such as Brasília have been criticised by their own residents for lacking the street life that older cities have long possessed.
C) Soviet collectivisation caused famine in regions where local cultivators had warned officials that the central plans were unworkable and harmful.
D) Forest historians disagree about how far yields in the Saxon plantations actually declined in the later rotations of replanting after the first.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 6: customary arrangements could be oppressive and legibility could liberate individuals from them; registration extending women’s rights is a direct example. The other options support Scott’s or Jacobs’s side or are neutral.

questions.passage:
A state cannot govern what it cannot see. questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author’s concluding position?
options: A) Legibility is a tool of domination that societies should resist in favour of the customary arrangements it displaces wherever they still exist.
B) Legibility is a neutral technology whose effects are determined solely by the technical quality of the records that are produced by officials.
C) Whether legibility helps or harms depends on who holds the map, for what purpose, and with what accountability.
D) Local knowledge and central knowledge are complementary, so states should replace registers with community consultation entirely and at once.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The final sentences: 'not whether a society should be legible but to whom, for what purpose, and with what accountability' and 'a map is neither friendly nor hostile'. The alternatives are one-sided or replace the author’s conditions with an absolute.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Antibiotics do not create such variants; they merely select them.
2. Any population of bacteria contains a few variants that happen to tolerate the drug.
3. Antibiotic resistance, in this sense, is evolution observed at the speed of a clinic.
4. When the drug removes their competitors, those variants multiply and inherit the tolerance.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states that tolerant variants already exist, 1 clarifies that the drug only selects them, 4 explains how they multiply once competitors are removed, and 3 ('in this sense') draws the concluding comparison with evolution.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Imitation by the many therefore destroys the very distinction the few were paying for.
2. Veblen observed that people sometimes buy such goods precisely because they are expensive.
3. This logic explains why fashions among the elite are abandoned once they are widely copied.
4. Status goods derive their value partly from their scarcity.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 introduces status goods and scarcity, 2 ('such goods') adds Veblen's observation, 1 ('therefore') draws the consequence of imitation, and 3 ('this logic') applies it to fashion.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The compromise satisfied neither camp, yet it endured for decades.
2. Its durability, historians suggest, lay precisely in its ambiguity.
3. Each side could thereby read into the text the meaning that suited it.
4. For the framers had deliberately left the key clause vague.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 1 states the puzzle, 2 ('its durability') gives the explanation (ambiguity), 4 ('For the framers...') supplies the reason for the ambiguity, and 3 ('thereby') shows its effect on each side.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Some studies suggest that habitual users retain a weaker spatial memory of familiar cities than those who navigate by landmarks.
2. A map that marks every path, however, tempts the traveller to stop looking at the terrain.
3. The convenience is real and not to be dismissed.
4. Navigation software has made getting lost a rarity.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 states the benefit, 3 affirms it, 2 ('however') introduces the drawback in general terms, and 1 gives the supporting evidence for that drawback.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Yet the borrowing is rarely one-way.
2. English has absorbed thousands of words from the languages it met through trade and empire.
3. Words such as 'bungalow' and 'shampoo' arrived from Indian languages during colonial rule.
4. Indian languages, in turn, now absorb English vocabulary every day.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states the general fact, 3 gives examples, 1 ('Yet') turns to the reverse direction, and 4 ('in turn') completes the two-way picture.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Charles Goodhart observed that statistical regularities tend to collapse once pressure is placed on them for control purposes. Teachers evaluated by test scores may narrow instruction to the tested material; hospitals judged by waiting times may reclassify patients; police judged by recorded crime may under-record it. In each case the indicator improves while the underlying quantity it was meant to capture stagnates or worsens, because the indicator has been separated from the behaviour it once tracked.'
options: A) Test scores, waiting times and recorded crime figures are inherently unreliable measures that institutions should stop collecting altogether from now on.
B) Teachers, hospitals and police forces routinely falsify their data in order to avoid scrutiny and to secure additional public funding for themselves.
C) Statistical regularities collapse whenever they are measured, regardless of whether anyone has an incentive to influence the outcome being measured.
D) Once an indicator becomes a target, people optimise the indicator itself, so it stops reflecting the reality it was meant to track.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph's point is that targeting an indicator detaches it from what it tracked. The other options condemn measurement itself, allege routine falsification, or claim measurement alone breaks regularities.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Ricardo’s theory shows that two countries can gain from trade even when one is more efficient at producing everything, provided each specialises in goods for which its opportunity cost is lower. The gains, however, are aggregate: within each country, workers in import-competing industries may lose, and the theory’s prescriptions depend on the assumption that displaced workers can move to expanding sectors at modest cost, an assumption that regional evidence has increasingly questioned.'
options: A) Comparative advantage raises aggregate welfare, but gains are uneven and rely on displaced workers being able to move.
B) Ricardo proved that a country more efficient in every good gains nothing from trade, since it could produce everything at home more cheaply.
C) Free trade harms workers in every industry, so the theory’s prescriptions have been decisively refuted by regional evidence from recent decades.
D) Trade gains arise only when each country specialises in goods for which its absolute costs are lowest, whatever the opportunity costs involved.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The correct option keeps both parts: aggregate gains and the uneven, assumption-dependent distribution. The others reverse Ricardo, overstate the harm to 'every' industry, or confuse absolute with comparative advantage.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Peer review is often described as the gatekeeper of scientific quality, yet studies suggest that reviewers agree about the merits of a manuscript only modestly more often than chance would predict. Defenders argue that it nonetheless screens out the grossest errors and improves the manuscripts that survive; critics note that it is slow, unpaid and prone to favour conventional work, and that fraud and irreproducibility slip through. The evidence, in short, supports a modest role for peer review as a filter rather than the certification of truth it is sometimes taken to be.'
options: A) Peer review is worthless, since reviewers agree only rarely and therefore cannot screen out even the grossest errors in submitted manuscripts.
B) Peer review is a modest, imperfect filter against error, not the certification of truth it is sometimes taken to be.
C) Peer review has been abolished in most journals because it is slow, unpaid and biased in favour of unconventional research over conventional work.
D) Reviewers agree about manuscripts far more often than chance would predict, which shows that peer review reliably certifies scientific truth.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph concludes that peer review has 'a modest role as a filter'. The alternatives call it worthless, invent its abolition (and reverse the bias), or reverse the finding on reviewer agreement.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'The Lindy effect suggests that the longer a non-perishable thing such as a book or an idea has survived, the longer its likely remaining life. This is not because age confers virtue but because survival over time is itself evidence of having withstood many challenges. The inference, however, fails for perishable things such as humans, for whom ________.'
options: A) longer survival to date predicts a still longer remaining lifespan, exactly as it does for books and ideas of great age in the same way
B) the challenges survived carry no information whatever about how much longer any living thing is likely to endure in the future
C) each additional year survived brings a person closer to a biologically limited lifespan
D) age confers virtue in proportion to the number of years lived, so that the oldest people are also the most reliable judges of truth
questions.explanation: Explanation: For perishable things the biological limit dominates: each year survived brings the individual nearer the end. The other options repeat the Lindy inference, over-generalise to 'any living thing', or reintroduce the 'age confers virtue' idea the paragraph rejected.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Economists distinguish between the interest rate a lender charges and the return the lender actually receives after inflation. When inflation is unexpectedly high, borrowers gain and lenders lose, because ________.'
options: A) nominal interest rates rise automatically to compensate lenders before the unexpected inflation has actually occurred in the economy
B) lenders can always renegotiate the terms of existing loans once the higher rate of inflation becomes known to all the parties
C) borrowers must repay a larger real sum than they originally borrowed because prices fall after the loans have been made to them
D) loans are repaid in money that has lost purchasing power since the loan was made
questions.explanation: Explanation: Unexpected inflation erodes the real value of the fixed nominal repayment, so borrowers gain and lenders lose. The other options describe expected inflation, unavailable renegotiation, or deflation, which would reverse the result.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'LUGUBRIOUS':
options: A) Doleful
B) Jocular
C) Ebullient
D) Ribald
questions.explanation: Explanation: Lugubrious means mournful, gloomy; 'doleful' is its synonym. 'Jocular' and 'ebullient' are its opposites.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'CAPRICIOUS':
options: A) Whimsical
B) Erratic
C) Steadfast
D) Unpredictable
questions.explanation: Explanation: Capricious means given to sudden, unaccountable changes of mood; 'steadfast' (firm, unwavering) is the antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'PUGNACIOUS':
options: A) Conciliatory
B) Combative
C) Indolent
D) Bashful
questions.explanation: Explanation: Pugnacious means eager to fight or argue; 'combative' matches. 'Conciliatory' is the antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'ABSTEMIOUS':
options: A) Temperate
B) Restrained
C) Ascetic
D) Indulgent
questions.explanation: Explanation: Abstemious means sparing in eating, drinking or pleasures; 'indulgent' is the antonym. The other options are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'SPURIOUS':
options: A) Bogus
B) Authentic
C) Legitimate
D) Verifiable
questions.explanation: Explanation: Spurious means not genuine or false; 'bogus' is the synonym. The others are its opposites.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The critic’s ________ remarks, delivered with evident relish, wounded the young author far more than honest disagreement would have.'
options: A) benign
B) effusive
C) caustic
D) tepid
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Caustic' means biting and sarcastic, which fits remarks delivered with relish that wound. 'Benign' and 'effusive' would not wound; 'tepid' means lukewarm.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'Although the treaty was hailed as a ________ achievement, critics dismissed it as merely ________.'
options: A) trivial; historic
B) landmark; cosmetic
C) tentative; decisive
D) genuine; authentic
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Although' signals contrast: praise as a landmark against the criticism that it is only cosmetic. The other pairs fail the contrast or are internally inconsistent.

questions.question:
Choose the correct idiom meaning:
'To burn one’s bridges' means to:
options: A) celebrate a success with a lavish public display
B) complete a difficult task well ahead of the deadline
C) abandon a costly project after years of effort
D) cut off every possibility of retreat
questions.explanation: Explanation: The image is of destroying the way back; the idiom means acting so as to make retreat impossible.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which the word 'DISINTERESTED' is used correctly (in its standard sense):
options: A) The judge, disinterested in the outcome, ruled purely on the law.
B) He was so disinterested in the lecture that he yawned throughout it.
C) Disinterested in sport, she rarely watched a match on television.
D) The disinterested child ignored the toys her parents had bought.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Disinterested' means impartial, having no stake in the result; 'uninterested' means lacking interest. Only the judge sentence uses it in the standard sense.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'One of the many reasons why the project failed ________ poor planning.'
options: A) were
B) was
C) are
D) have been
questions.explanation: Explanation: The subject is 'one' (singular), not 'reasons'; the past context requires 'was'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'The teacher, along with her students, (A) / were invited (B) / to attend (C) / the ceremony (D).'
options: A) The teacher, along with her students
B) were invited
C) to attend
D) the ceremony
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Along with her students' is parenthetical and does not change the number of the subject 'teacher', so the verb should be 'was invited'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) The new model is far superior than the old one in every respect.
B) The new model is far more superior to the old one.
C) The new model is far superior to the old one.
D) The new model is far superior from the old one.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Superior' takes 'to', not 'than' or 'from', and is already comparative, so 'more superior' is redundant.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'If I ________ you, I would not sign the agreement without reading it.'
options: A) were
B) was
C) am
D) had been
questions.explanation: Explanation: A hypothetical present condition takes the subjunctive 'were' for all persons.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) There were less complaints this year than last year.
B) There was fewer complaints this year than last.
C) There were much less of complaints this year than last.
D) There were fewer complaints this year than last.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns ('complaints'), with a plural verb 'were'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'She has (A) / been working (B) / in this firm (C) / since five years (D).'
options: A) She has
B) been working
C) in this firm
D) since five years
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time; for a period of time, 'for' is required: 'for five years'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'The lawyer’s argument was inconsistent ________ the evidence.'
options: A) to
B) for
C) with
D) against
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Inconsistent' correctly pairs with 'with'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) I saw him yesterday at the station near my office.
B) I have seen him yesterday at the station.
C) She has lived in this city since 2010 without a break.
D) By the time we arrived, the film had already started.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A definite past time ('yesterday') requires the simple past ('I saw'), not the present perfect.
